thread.title: SCHB: This Chart Helps Me Sleep At Night - For Now - Schwab U.S. Broad Market ETF (NYSEARCA:SCHB)

author: Dividend Seeker
title: SCHB: This Chart Helps Me Sleep At Night - For Now - Schwab U.S. Broad Market ETF (NYSEARCA:SCHB)
text:
Main Thesis The purpose of this article is to articulate why I believe the Schwab U.S. Broad Market ( SCHB ) fund is an attractive investment at its current market price. Despite some volatility, equities remain my preferred strategy for the second half of 2018. Trade fears had ramped up, but the market has remained resilient, which tells me investors who move to the sidelines now may miss out. For the most part, corporate earnings are expected to be strong and that, coupled with strong employment figures, tells me the market has a solid underlying basis for continued gains. Finally, while a flattening yield curve continues to concern me, this trend has not yet pushed the curve in to negative territory, which is a key warning signal of a potential recession. Barring that occurrence, stocks should continue to push higher.
Background First, a little background on SCHB. SCHB is managed by Charles Schwab and its stated objective is "to track as closely as possible, before fees and expenses, the total return of the Dow Jones U.S. Broad Stock Market Index". Currently, SCHB is trading at $67.87/share and yields around 1.65% annually, based on its current share price and last four distributions. My last review of SCHB was back in April, when I continued to recommend exposure to equities. Since that time, SCHB is up over 8%. Furthermore, SCHB actually bests the performance of the S&P 500 over the past three months, as illustrated by the graph below:
Source: CNBC
While there are numerous headwinds on the horizon, I continue to believe underlying fundamentals of the economy are strong, and expect further gains for SCHB for the second half of 2018. Therefore, I remain long SCHB, and I will explain why in detail below.
Yield Curve - Not Time To Worry, Yet To begin, let us start with an interest rate discussion. With rising interest rates, an earnings season in full swing, and escalating trade disputes, it can be hard to know what to focus on. For me, while all those topics are of note, interest rates should remain an important consideration for investors. While increasing interest rates will not in and of themselves send stocks lower, they will likely pressure some sectors more than others. Furthermore, without strong underlying metrics, higher interest rates can stall an otherwise growing economy. While I don't think that scenario will pan out in 2018, it is important to note that the yield curve continues to flatten, with means the gap between yields of short-term and long-term bonds is shrinking. This is a warning sign, because it points to investor's concerns about long-term growth. Importantly, an inverted yield curve (when the spread between the 10-year and 2-year is negative) has been a reliable sign of a forthcoming recession, as illustrated by the graph below:
Source: Kiplinger
As you can see from the graph, a negative spread foreshadowed each recession over the past forty years. And the takeaway to be aware of here is the yield curve continues to move south. So why does this chart help me sleep at night? Plainly, because we are not in negative territory yet, and a positive spread between the 10-year and 2-year remains. This tells me while the market is concerned, it is not sold on the idea that future growth will stall, it is simply pointing out a risk at this point. Seeing as how this metric has been reliable in its indication of a recession for the long-term, I am sleeping soundly knowing that we are not in that territory yet. My takeaway is, we still have time to profit from stocks and, just as importantly, we still have time to see longer-term rates edge up along with shorter-term rates. This could happen if investors become more convinced about long-term growth, or if the Fed slows the pace of interest rate hikes over the next 3-12 months. Therefore, while this is a chart I will be watching with a keen eye going forward, for now it tells me not lose any sleep over my equity exposure just yet.
Employment Data Is Strong For further guidance on how strong the underlying economy really is, let us take a look at the most recent employment report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The largest takeaway for me is that the U.S. continues to see job growth, expanding on a multi-year trend, as illustrated by the chart below:
Source: BLS
However, while total nonfarm payroll employment increased by 213,000 last month, it is important to note the unemployment rate actually rose to 4.0% (up from 3.9%). While the rate increasing is not normally a positive sign, in this case any negative perception should be muted because it was a result of increasing labor force participation. This is a positive sign, because it means more people are confident about obtaining employment, and are choosing to re-enter the labor force. Therefore, while we saw an increase in employment figures, June also saw the labor force grow by 601,000, which in turn raised the unemployment rate. This was directly the result of the labor force participation rate heading higher, clocking in at 62.9%, which is up from 62.7% in May. Ultimately, I would love to see this figure move higher still, but the fact that we are moving in the right direction gives me a lot of confidence. As long as this trend remains in-tact, consumer spending should remain a driver of economic growth, and that bodes well for stocks.
IT Exposure Is Driving Out-Performance An important point when considering SCHB as an investment option is the outlook for the Information Technology (IT) sector, as it makes up over a quarter of the fund's portfolio, as illustrated by the graphic below:
Source: Schwab
Fortunately, this large exposure has been benefitting the fund, and is part of the reason for the slight out-performance over the S&P 500. The IT sector has beaten the broader market by a handsome margin since the start of the year, as illustrated by the graph below (the dark blue line represents the IT sector, the light blue line represents the S&P 500):
Source: Fidelity
In fact, the top four holdings of SCHB are all technology firms, with Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), and Facebook ( FB ), representing over 10% of the fund alone. These are companies that are cash-rich, and have benefitted immensely from recent tax reform. Notably, Apple is known to have one of the largest cash reserves held overseas, and saw the value of these holdings increase when the tax repatriation law was passed (assuming that cash would have been taxed at the previous corporate tax rate). With strong balance sheets, this sector should hold up well if we experience market volatility, or if earnings slow.
Furthermore, this sector will broadly benefit as companies continue to look to technology upgrades to improve efficiency, combat rising costs, and remain cutting edge in the eyes of the consumer. According to IT consultancy firm, Gartner, IT spending will show strong growth this year, and further growth is expected in 2019 as well, as illustrated by the chart below:
Source: Gartner
While growth is notably expected to slow from 2018, an expected growth rate of almost 3% is quite good, and should continue to help the bulk of companies within this sector. Couple this with continued demand for IT consumer products (think iPhones) and I see a lot of reasons to stay long this sector.
Bottom-line While the market has seen volatility recently, my outlook for equities in 2018 remains positive. Investors who stayed the course throughout this year have been rewarded, and I think the second half of 2018 will play out in a similar way. For instance, rather than selling on trade war fears, use those drops to add to equity positions. And a great way to do this is with SCHB, which is a low-cost fund which tracks the total stock market. While rising interest rates are a concern, economic growth persists, and employment gains should hopefully offset the Fed's small, gradual increases. While the flattening yield curve remains a concern, the curve remains positive, indicating a recession is not likely on the immediate horizon. For now, I will ignore the short-term noise and focus on the positive, such as positive employment figures and strong corporate earnings. Therefore, I remain long equities, and continue to recommend investors consider initiating positions in SCHB at this time.
Disclosure: I am/we are long SCHB.
